source.title: Safety Drift After Fine-Tuning: Evidence from High-Stakes Domains
source.authors: Emaan Bilal Khan; Amy Winecoff; Miranda Bogen; Dylan Hadfield-Menell

page_placements.theme: Safety conclusions depend on metrics, judges and output validity

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign fine-tuning changes safety behavior, but uses domain-specific training and broad safety benchmarks rather than the original studies' precise fine-tuning and refusal-rate setups.
record.gate_note: The paper reports benchmark-level outcomes and aggregate summaries, as well as some individual model-method examples. Cited results from other studies are not recorded. It does not test harmful-data fine-tuning, first-token KL, compliant-prefix attacks, or safety-localizing weight edits.
record.test_reason: The study measures how often and how strongly benign medical and legal fine-tuning changes responses to harmful prompts (HEx-PHI, MLCommons, MedSafetyBench), relative to base models. Phase II fine-tunes four instruction-tuned bases under controlled conditions. This is a new, realistic domain-adaptation setting bearing on V2, not the originals' Alpaca/Dolly/identity-shift recipes, so T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that benign domain fine-tuning produces large, heterogeneous, often mixed-sign changes in measured safety. They find that method, base family and update magnitude predict little, that conclusions depend on the benchmark and judge setup, and that fine-tuned models need re-evaluation rather than inheriting base-model safety.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benign medical and legal domain datasets, ecological model comparisons, and controlled full fine-tuning/LoRA/QLoRA; it does not use harmful-example fine-tuning or measure refusal loss as the primary outcome.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary across safety benchmarks, domain, base model, and fine-tuning method. Adding examples to the HEx-PHI judging template also changes measured results; 25% of medical results reverse sign.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized L2 parameter distance does not systematically predict safety drift (|ρ|<0.25). On legal HEx-PHI, smaller updates correlated with more degradation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The magnitude of a fine-tuning update does not predict the size or direction of safety change.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding score examples to the HEx-PHI judge template reversed the sign of 25% of medical base-vs-fine-tune differences, with outputs held fixed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured fine-tuning safety drift is sensitive to the judge rubric's implementation.

fits_no_version.finding: SafeLawBench (legal correctness) degraded for 92% of controlled legal configurations, while 73% of ecological legal models moved toward safer behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain fine-tuning shifts domain-specific correctness and safety measures in benchmark-dependent directions.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society
record.problems: The authors report substantial benchmark disagreement and note that several evaluations lack external validation against ground-truth harms. Ecological model comparisons involve models with differing and often undocumented data and training procedures, limiting causal interpretation. The controlled phase uses one dataset per domain and four instruction-tuned base models. The judging-template experiment shows that evaluation choices can alter measured outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional aggregate and figure-level benchmark comparisons, correlations, and lineage statistics. These were not separately extracted where they did not directly measure the harmful-compliance behavior named by V2, or where they would duplicate the benchmark-specific aggregate outcomes recorded above.

untested.parts: Carefully selected benign examples (e.g., benign data chosen to break safety); small doses of a few to a few hundred examples (runs used 250k/525k-example datasets for 1 epoch); closed-API models; the originals' exact refusal/harmfulness-rate setup.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No localization of safety in weights. The L2-distance analysis measures update magnitude only.
No test of what causes shallowness.
No deepening method trained or evaluated.

missing.what: Phase I correlation between base-model unsafety and drift (Pearson r≈−0.55, p<0.001). More strongly aligned bases were more likely to degrade, which bears directly on V2 for safety-trained models.
Phase I observation that consistent improvement was more common when unaligned bases were fine-tuned than instruction-tuned ones. This is needed to split Phase I by base type.
Controlled legal fine-tuning: HEx-PHI showed method-dependent sign reversals and SORRY-Bench (legal refusal) frequently improved. 42% mixed-sign drift on direct unsafe-behaviour benchmarks.
Per-model, per-method HEx-PHI and Trident drift values for controlled legal runs, and HEx-PHI values for medical runs.
Lineage results: median absolute drift rose from 7pp at the first fine-tune to 13pp at the second. 60–86% of lineages reversed sign between stages, and HEx-PHI SD rose by 9.75.

record.verdict_notes: Only Phase II, with four instruction-tuned bases, cleanly tests V2. Phase I pools unaligned and aligned bases with undocumented recipes. Fine-tuning used large datasets (250k/525k) for 1 epoch at lr 2e-5. CARES penalizes over-refusal, and SafeLawBench/SORRY-Bench legal subsets measure correctness or refusal of legitimate legal queries, so they are not clean harmful-compliance measures. The authors cite Qi et al. papers as prior work. This study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning or few-to-hundreds-example dose is tested.
Tests benign domain fine-tuning, not the specific refusal rate alone; does not test carefully selected benign examples or a few-to-hundreds-example training dose.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
No compliant-prefix, suffix, or decoding bypass experiment.
Does not identify or edit a small set of weights or ranks that carries safety behavior.
Does not test why safety would be shallow or whether data or objective produces shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to deepen safety across response tokens.

rows.subject: medical fine-tuned models (Phase I aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared deployed medical fine-tuned models with their corresponding base models.
rows.value: −1.5 to −6.6 percentage points, depending on the benchmark
rows.note: Aggregate range across benchmarks; the reported median changes indicate lower, not higher, unsafe-response rates.
rows.check: The Phase I aggregate mixes unaligned pretrained bases (e.g., Llama-2-7b, Mistral-7B-v0.1) with instruction-tuned bases. V2 concerns safety-trained models. The authors say improvement was more common for unaligned bases, so the pooled median cannot test V2.

rows.subject: medical fine-tuned models (Phase I aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared deployed medical fine-tuned models with their corresponding base models.
rows.measure: share of models with lower unsafe-response rates than their base
rows.note: The paper says roughly 60% of fine-tuned models showed lower unsafe-response rates on any given benchmark.
rows.check: Same mixed-base problem as R1. It also pools CARES (which penalizes over-refusal) with harmful-prompt benchmarks.

rows.subject: legal fine-tuned models (Phase I aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared deployed legal fine-tuned models with their corresponding base models.
rows.measure: direction of change in unsafe behavior
rows.note: Models were split nearly evenly between improvement and degradation across most benchmarks.
rows.check: The condition is wrong. The 47% vs 53% split is stated for 'most benchmarks, particularly SORRY-Bench and Trident', not for HEx-PHI/MLCommons/Trident. The aggregate also mixes unaligned and aligned bases.

rows.subject: legal fine-tuned models (Phase I aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared deployed legal fine-tuned models with their corresponding base models.
rows.measure: share of models moving toward safer behavior
rows.note: The paper reports a safer direction for most models on this measure.
rows.check: SafeLawBench is a pairwise rating of legal correctness against ground truth, not harmful compliance. It does not measure what V2 names.

rows.subject: controlled medical fine-tuning configurations (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on the medical domain dataset using controlled training configurations.
rows.measure: median change in safety score, with positive values standardized as degradation
rows.note: The paper reports the in-domain benchmark improvement as a reduction in unsafe behavior.
rows.check: Correct as recorded. MedSafetyBench measures compliance with medically unethical requests, and the median improved 12.2pp.

rows.subject: controlled medical fine-tuning configurations (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on the medical domain dataset using controlled training configurations.
rows.note: The paper also states that 100% of medical configurations degraded on this benchmark.

rows.subject: controlled medical fine-tuning configurations (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on the medical domain dataset using controlled training configurations.
rows.measure: share of configurations improving on the in-domain benchmarks
rows.note: This aggregate improvement contrasts with the general-purpose benchmark result.
rows.check: The state should be reversed, not partial. 83% of configurations became safer on the in-domain benchmarks, the opposite of V2's direction.

relationships.condition: Phase II controlled fine-tuning of instruction-tuned 7–9B bases, general-purpose harmful-prompt benchmark MLCommons (LlamaGuard judge), medical and legal domains
relationships.reason: Every configuration degraded. The medical median was +26.4pp (100% degraded), Gemma-QLoRA +45pp, and the legal mean +19.8pp (R6, R9, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Every configuration degraded, with a median rise of 26.4 points in the medical domain, 45 points for Gemma with QLoRA, and a mean rise of 19.8 points in the legal domain.
